title: Trump confirms he switched planes after Nato summit because of possible threat
description: Figure caption, Watch: Trump tells reporters why he switched planesBySareen HabeshianUpdated 5 hours agoPresident Donald Trump has confirmed that he s
body: Figure caption, Watch: Trump tells reporters why he switched planesBySareen HabeshianUpdated 5 hours agoPresident Donald Trump has confirmed that he secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month due to a possible threat."I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane," Trump told reporters. "I just have to do what they say."The revelation comes after reports that Trump boarded Air Force One on 8 July in view of television cameras, before hiding in a catering truck to be transported to a military aircraft.The last-minute switch has raised questions about whether those left on the decoy plane were in danger, but Trump said on Tuesday the jet he boarded instead could have been at "greater risk... because that would be the plane, I think, that they would be more likely to go for."Officials told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the US had detected a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane. The New York Times reported that US intelligence had information of a person near the Nato summit who had been seen with a shoulder-fired missile.Journalists and some White House staff on board did not know the US president had been smuggled out as part of an elaborate ruse in response to a possible Iranian threat.Figure caption, Watch: Was Donald Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?Trump has previously said he was Iran's "number one target" during the summit in Ankara."I guess there was a threat out there," the president said during a visit aboard Air Force One to an event in Ohio on Tuesday. "I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats."He added: "I have a lot of threats that you don't know about."The clandestine manoeuvre last month came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran following a breakdown of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end the war.Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar, but announced that he would leave on the old Air Force One "for old time's sake".On 8 July, footage showed him boarding the presidential jet at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he slipped off Air Force One on to a catering truck that had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded.He was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president.Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the C-32A separately using external stairs in an effort to make the flight appear normal, according to the newspaper.Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board.A media pool producer who was on the plane said they found it unusual when they were told to keep the window shades down. A photographer briefly opened a shade and reportedly was quickly told to close it.The producer's comments were detailed in a report from the White House Correspondents' Association on Tuesday. They also noted there appeared to have been two catering trucks at both the front and back of the plane when the press arrived, and that the media van had been too far back in the motorcade at the airport be able to take a photo of the president boarding.Figure caption, Watch: Washington Post and AP reporters reveal details of plane swap over Iran threatTechnically "Air Force One" is the call sign for any aircraft carrying the US president. But on this occasion, the C-32A used the call sign "Reach 18", while the aircraft carrying the journalists continued to use "AF1" in order to keep up the ruse.Remaining on the original aircraft were members of Trump's cabinet, according to the New York Times. The outlet, citing two anonymous officials, reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were on board.Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet.The president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington.During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap.Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said at the time: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with."He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list".Jose Zamora, regional director for the Americas for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said in a statement that the Trump administration "has a responsibility to ensure that journalists covering the president are not unnecessarily exposed to danger"."Reporters should be informed of credible security threats so they can make informed decisions about their safety," he added.Figure caption, Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump?Additional reporting by Jessica Rawnsley

schema.headline: Trump confirms he switched planes after Nato summit because of possible threat

title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief warns
description: The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or
body: The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong"."Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure. "I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs across the UK signed a letter to the prime minister urging him to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.They called for called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, adding: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."They also welcomed Burnham's intervention on Tuesday, when he said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, in January could be stopped.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp told BBC Breakfast the early release plans had "put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system".He urged Burnham to "pay attention and listen" to the senior police officers, adding he had "never seen every police constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".Philip and Nick Timothy, the Conservative shadow justice secretary, wrote to Burnham on Tuesday urging him to introduce emergency primary legislation in September to amend the Sentencing Act 2026.The letter said grooming gang perpetrators, including those convicted of indecent assault, and those convicted of the manslaughter of an emergency worker should be exempt from the early release scheme.Probation officers help former prisoners with housing, employment and access to benefits once in the community, and help protect the public by assessing the risk of further offending.Their workload will increase substantially when more offenders - some of whom will have been convicted of violent offences - are released months earlier than planned as part of the Sentencing Act.According to the chief inspector, probation caseload has increased by 8% over the last two years. Much of that is down to a separate early release scheme which was implemented in 2024 after prisons nearly reached full capacity. That scheme has led to tens of thousands of offenders being let out sooner.When asked what risk the additional early releases due to start in the autumn could pose to the public, Jones said "that could be a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder".One probation officer told the BBC the upcoming releases had put him and his colleagues into "a state of panic"."We can't cope with this - we've been saying that to anybody who will listen. "At the minute I think it's pure panic in terms of where we're at. I don't understand how there can be this level of pressure put on us."The worst that can happen is that things are missed, plans aren't put into place and we don't give people the level of service they need and that leads to serious further offences."That leads to death under supervision."In a statement, an MoJ spokesperson said the department had exceeded its recruitment target for last year, with 1,389 trainee probation officers starting. The spokesperson said this is "making sure the Probation Service has the resource it needs to keep dangerous offenders under closer surveillance than ever before"."The Sentencing Act is restoring order to a prison system left on the brink of collapse, while our record £700m investment in probation and community punishment is ensuring staff have the resources, powers, and technology they need to manage offenders safely in the community," the spokesperson added.On Tuesday, probation officers voted in favour of strike action over the scheme, with probation union Napo saying 90% of its members had backed potential industrial action."This ballot wasn't about members being too busy," Napo national chair Ben Cockburn said. "It was professionals warning they cannot protect the public properly when there are not enough people to do the work."The MoJ said it was "disappointed" by the ballot outcome.Inspectorate reports published between January and March 2026 highlight staffing gaps in probation, a lack of experience, significant issues with information sharing, as well as "the burden placed on overstretched staff by large-scale change programmes".As of March, there were 5,554 full-time equivalent probation officers, a shortfall of 1,556 against the target staffing level of 7,110.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there will be a presumption that all offenders released as part of the new laws will be tagged and have longer periods of supervision. This will mean more responsibility on probation staff."Electronic tagging has been talked about as a key part of the arrangement but actually all that provides you with is information to inform their understanding of what is going on and then to act upon that when necessary, and I'm not sure the systems are there and robust enough to assist the probation officer when they're doing their work," Jones said."I've previously said that it would be a good idea to look at the overall workload of probation and consider what are the essential things that they need to be doing, not what's desirable.""It's a matter of desirable work that I want the probation service to be doing."But with a probation service that probably has a vacancy rate of 20-25%, what can they realistically do."On Tuesday, the prime minister said he was "increasingly confident" that work to add space in the prison system "will allow us to reduce the number of people released early".It comes as Burnham is facing growing pressure to ensure the killers of PC Andrew Harper are not released as part of the scheme. Downing Street had earlier warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from early release. But after an outcry, Burnham ordered the justice secretary to find a way to bar Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers from the scheme, and the prime minister has now said he is "confident" they can be excluded.The letter welcomed the prime minister's intervention, adding: "This provides an opportunity not only to examine every lawful avenue in PC Andrew Harper's case, but to ensure similar concerns do not arise again."

schema.headline: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief warns

title: Woman assaulted by double murderer Simon Levy says nightmare became 'real life' when police let him attack again
description: A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on
body: A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on to kill and attack more women.Laura, whose surname we are not using, said she had been trying to protect other women by reporting Levy in 2018, but feels betrayed by what he was later allowed to do after being released from jail.Levy was convicted on Friday of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins and raping another woman in London in 2025. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.He was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the Tube in London between 2023 and 2025.Police, prosecutors and the courts made a series of disastrous decisions that left Levy free. He attacked 14 more women before being taken off the streets, despite being a sex offender who was monitored by the Met Police.Levy was a registered sex offender because he sexually assaulted Laura – and a separate victim - in summer 2018.Laura says that Levy is "evil" and that his attack "completely changed my life".But she now realises that what she would "think about, dream about, have nightmares about was actually happening - he was actually still out preying on vulnerable women".Waiving her anonymity, she said she had been trying to protect other women by ensuring that Levy was jailed."I feel like when I reported it, I was doing the right thing and I thought I was doing it to protect other women."I feel absolutely devastated for all of those women that have been affected by him – and the families."Laura says she feels let down by the whole criminal justice system including the Met Police, the courts and judges who bailed Levy, as well as the Crown Prosecution Service."They're all as guilty for allowing him to continue to do what he was doing", she says."They could have prevented so many women from being hurt. "They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."Laura encountered Levy while with a friend travelling to the Notting Hill Carnival on the London Underground in August 2018. He latched onto them and followed them to the carnival. He then subjected her to a serious sexual assault.Laura says she forced Levy off and became "hysterical" and started "crying". With her friend, they tried to escape Levy but he kept following them. Eventually, a group of men chased him off after she told people what had happened.But when she tried to report the crime to police officers, she was turned away.She says two Met officers told her that they "were busy with other, more urgent, things".A third, female officer eventually took her details, but Laura says the officer didn't make sure she was safe, or look for Levy that day, despite Laura and her friend having a photo of him."There was a lot more things they could have done to make me feel supported", she says.Challenged on the response to Laura at the carnival, the Met Police said: "We are sorry the victim felt unsupported in this case and don't underestimate the impact this incident had on her. "A crime report was created the following day with a wide range of enquiries carried out. Levy was identified, arrested and later convicted."After later being contacted by officers, Laura gave a statement 15 days after the attack, and attended an ID parade the next year. It took three years for Levy to go to court. In 2021 he was convicted of sexually assaulting her, as well as another woman he had assaulted a month before Laura.He was jailed for three years, but released on licence despite sexually assaulting a prison officer.Laura found out Simon Levy was going to be on trial for two murders when she Googled his name earlier this year."My heart dropped in my stomach when I read that", she says.Laura says she was also shocked to discover that Levy had already been investigated for allegedly sexually assaulting another woman in 2017. He was not charged at the time, something now viewed as a mistake by the CPS and the Met."Had they charged him in 2017, I may not have even ever had to go to court. I may never have been assaulted, ever".She says there should be a societal change in the approach to male violence against women and girls."They need to look at everything, all of it, because they could have prevented so many women from being hurt. "They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."She adds: "I hope that other victims in the future will be believed, will be dealt with differently, will be listened to straightaway, and I just hope that there's change".BBC Action Line: If you have been affected by issues in this story, find out what support is available here.Do you have information about this story? Contact us on email daniel.desimone@bbc.co.uk or via the Signal messaging app @investigation.56

schema.headline: Woman assaulted by double murderer Simon Levy says nightmare became 'real life' when police let him attack again

title: Poorest areas should not house all asylum seekers, says Andy Burnham
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has suggested that wealthier areas of the UK should house more asylum seekers."We cannot have a situation where it's only
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has suggested that wealthier areas of the UK should house more asylum seekers."We cannot have a situation where it's only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers," he told GB News , externalon Tuesday.His comments came in response to a question about protests which have taken place in the village of Piddington, Oxfordshire over plans to provide accommodation for asylum seekers on a nearby former military base. But shadow home secretary Chris Philp, responding to Burnham's comments, said: "We shouldn't be housing illegal immigrants anywhere – wealthy or not."Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised."I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said."We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.Speaking on BBC Breakfast on Wednesday morning, immigration minister Anna Turley said the number of hotels had gone from a peak of 400 under the Conservatives to 160 under Labour, and pledged all of them would close by 2029.Turley said the government had already saved £1bn by closing hotels and opening alternative, secure sites for asylum seekers, including two former military bases, student accommodation and former industrial sites around the country."I think this is about fairness and we won't be asking anybody to take more than they can, and we won't be asking anyone to take more than their fair share," she said."What we've seen in the past is places like Blackpool, and other communities around the country where housing is perhaps cheaper and more plentiful, have had to take more than their fair share of asylum seekers," she added."That's put a huge burden on local communities and created real civil unrest, so we want to make sure that we're managing the system much better in a more sustained way that's reducing the impact on local communities."It's important that everybody plays their fair share in that, and it's about making sure that no one community is more over-pressured or overburdened than others."Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country. "Andy Burnham just doesn't get it," he wrote on X."Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."Government statistics, external showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607). Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.He complained about the government's dispersal system and said Greater Manchester's public services could not continue to support "disproportionate" numbers of people compared with elsewhere in the country.Burnham at the time said the north-west of England was hosting 25% of the national population of asylum applicants who require housing and support - with Greater Manchester housing 70% of the region's numbers.The then-Home Secretary Sajid Javid replied by promising to work towards a fairer distribution.

schema.headline: Poorest areas should not house all asylum seekers, says Andy Burnham

title: Fifty police chiefs call for PM to prevent early release of PC Harper's killers
description: The police chiefs from Scotland, England, Wales and Northern Ireland also called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their senten
body: The police chiefs from Scotland, England, Wales and Northern Ireland also called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered - such as with the government's early release scheme, which was designed to reduce prison overcrowding.Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, will become eligible for release from custody after serving half of their sentences.In the letter, released on Tuesday evening, police chiefs said the early release of PC Harper's killers, and that of anyone involved in the death of an officer, could cast doubt over the "value placed on their service and sacrifice when they put themselves in harm's way to protect others".They outlined three requests of the prime minister, beginning with pursuing "every lawful option to determine whether the earlier release of those responsible for PC Andrew Harper's death can be prevented" - which Burnham has already pledged to do. Second, they called on the government to put greater consideration into the crimes committed by prisoners when altering their sentences.They wrote: "Where an offender has caused a death, committed exceptionally serious violence, or presents an ongoing risk to individuals or communities, there should be explicit consideration of public protection, victim impact and community safety before release arrangements are amended."This is not simply a question of punishment. It is a question of ensuring that public protection, victim confidence and community safety remain central to decisions that may substantially reduce the time an offender spends in custody."Lastly, the letter called for victims and bereaved families to be "properly considered whenever significant changes are made to sentencing or release arrangements".Around 5,000 people are expected to be released under the early release scheme, down from 6,000 after exemptions were previously announced for those convicted of the most serious crimes including rape, child sex offences and grooming.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said that in his 11 years of being an MP, including two years as police minister, he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".Speaking to BBC Breakfast, he added: "[The police chiefs] say that Labour's plans will put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system."Philp said the prime minister should "pay attention and listen to what they are saying".

schema.headline: Fifty police chiefs call for PM to prevent early release of PC Harper's killers

title: Solar eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low
description: At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves."I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not b
body: At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves."I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not baked goods driving queues out of the door - customers are here to buy eclipse glasses.They are among those hoping to catch a safe glimpse of Wednesday's solar eclipse - the UK's most significant since 1999 - but struggling to get their hands on the right gear.Experts have urged eclipse enthusiasts not to look directly at the Sun - with even brief exposure causing lasting damage - and to seek out specialist glasses instead.But online, pairs that meet safety specifications have all but sold out. Those still available either require a hefty next-day delivery fee or simply cannot arrive on time.Even the Royal Museums Greenwich - recommended as a reputable retailer by UK health officials - has sold out, citing an "unprecedented volume" of orders.Meanwhile, eclipse glasses have been turning up for sale in unexpected places as retailers try to capitalise on the demand."I Googled 'where can I get eclipse glasses but not through the post', because I realised I was too late," one customer waiting to buy three pairs at the bakery on Monday tells BBC Radio 4's PM programme."People have been struggling to find them all over," says another.A WhatsApp channel which advertises stock in corner shops - including some offering delivery - has attracted thousands of followers in a matter of days.Elsewhere, hopeful buyers in Reddit and Facebook threads are directed to online marketplaces, including for more expensive bulk purchases.Lily, 27, "posted on Instagram like everyone else did" after the glasses she ordered from Ebay failed to turn up."I had like three or four people replying saying, 'if you find out where to get some, let me know'."She said her best hope was a newsagents rumoured to be selling stock late on Tuesday evening - but hundreds of hopeful buyers were expected to turn up."I was like, I don't want to go to World War Three to find a pair of cardboard and plastic glasses. I accepted defeat."Luckily, a friend managed to get hold of some at the last minute on Tuesday in what she described as a "miracle". The UKHSA advises caution around products sold online. "If you're unsure whether a product is certified, don't use it."UKEclipse, an initiative set up by UK astronomers, also warns that major eclipses often attract "counterfeit and substandard" glasses and advises going through specialist retailers and organisations instead.The American Astronomical Society (AAS) urges eclipse chasers to check its list of manufacturers which it has confirmed test their glasses properly in a lab.Those who have managed to find a pair can try them ahead of time, it says, by testing them both inside and outside on a sunny day.In both settings, you should not be able to see anything other than perhaps very bright lights, including the Sun's reflection off a shiny surface, "which should appear very faint".If they pass that test, you can glance at the Sun - only for less than a second - and should only be able to see "a sharp-edged, round disk... that's comfortably bright, with a dark background all around it". "If your viewers pass all three tests, they are probably safe," it says.Even just a small part of the Sun breaking through the glasses can harm your eyes, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists has warned, adding that the safest way to watch the event is indirectly - such as through a livestream or broadcast."Crucially, the retina has no pain receptors, so people will not feel the damage as it happens," explains the college's president Mohamed Elalfy.The college reported around 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching 1999's eclipse - around 40% of those affected had looked at it for less than a minute.Anyone who notices a change in their vision after looking at the Sun should seek advice from an eye-care professional.You should not use binoculars, telescopes or the viewfinder of a camera even with your eclipse glasses on, because their magnifying effect can nullify the protection of the glasses and damage your sight.

schema.headline: Solar eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low

title: Aston Villa: Unai Emery chases his first Super Cup
description: Emery has suffered defeats by Real Madrid, Barcelona and Chelsea - the first two with Sevilla, and then losing on penalties to the Blues in Dublin wit
body: Emery has suffered defeats by Real Madrid, Barcelona and Chelsea - the first two with Sevilla, and then losing on penalties to the Blues in Dublin with Villarreal in 2021. A 5-4 extra-time loss to a Lionel Messi-inspired Barcelona in 2015 came a year after Cristiano Ronaldo scored twice to earn Real Madrid the trophy.Emery had already left for PSG by the time Sevilla lost the 2016 Super Cup to Real.But, at Red Bull Arena against his former side and with 6,000 Villa fans travelling, he has the chance to break his losing streak. "He [pointing to Villa captain John McGinn] was reminding me last week [about losing to Chelsea]," said Emery."Of course, it's an opportunity. A trophy is something that can give us a special moment. To play for trophies is, as a professional, our objective."PSG are the favourites but I am looking forward to playing, how we can test this match against PSG with our capacity?"As a coach, as a player, as a club, it's a trophy. It's one thing that makes us proud of how we are and how we arrive here."Carlo Ancelotti has five Super Cup crowns - two with AC Milan and three with Real Madrid - while Pep Guardiola is one behind after two wins with Barcelona and one each with Bayern Munich and Manchester City.Ancelotti's third title came when his Real side beat Emery's Sevilla in 2014.But, much like Sunday's Community Shield between Arsenal and Manchester City, is it not a glamorous pre-season friendly with a trophy? PSG midfielder Vitinha, who has won four Ligue 1 titles with the club, dismissed any suggestion the back-to-back Champions League winners treat it any differently, but did say PSG's "pre-season was a little short". "We're still hungry for victories, trophies. It's very difficult to maintain those levels but we're still hungry," said the Portugal international. Defender Marquinhos also insisted the competition remains important to ensure PSG - who were unhappy with the size of their dressing room at Red Bull Arena and given an additional one by Uefa - continue to win trophies. "Just because we've won things these past seasons, that doesn't mean it's easy. We know there'll be plenty of obstacles," he said."Personally, I want more, and each player in the squad is like that. We've all worked to get here, to arrive in the best condition."Wednesday's game between Villa and PSG is a repeat of the Champions League quarter-final from 2024-25. Trailing 3-1 from the first leg at Parc des Princes and falling 5-1 behind on aggregate in Birmingham, Villa were so close to pulling of a huge shock.They roared back from 2-0 down to win 3-2 on the night, eventually bowing out 5-4 on aggregate, and it was one of the biggest signs Emery had turned them into a side which could compete with Europe's best.It is something which has stuck in the minds of the PSG players, with Vitinha wary of Villa's threat."It was such a difficult test, especially the second half," said Vitinha."We'll be ready but we're conscious of how difficult it's going to be."Villa's line-up in Austria will have a drastically different look, just 484 days since that game. Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne and Youri Tielemans have been sold while Amadou Onana is out injured until next year.Fellow midfielder Boubacar Kamara is in the squad, but is only just returning from a serious knee injury he suffered in January.Emi Martinez, Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins have not travelled after playing at the World Cup, with Emery giving them a month off. It means there is a chance just four of the starters who faced the French champions 18 months ago will start for Villa. Five of the substitutes that night are also no longer at the club. For a team so settled and consistent as Villa under Emery that is a drastic change."A lot has changed in the eight years I've been here," said skipper McGinn. "When you are signing the best young English talent and players are performing at the highest level there will be interest. "We have a structure in place, standards and rules which have made us a success. I'm really excited about the new Aston Villa.  "We have our main core, the same manager, same methods and same desire to achieve more. A lot of people thought we reached a ceiling a couple of seasons ago and we proved them wrong."

schema.headline: Aston Villa: Unai Emery chases his first Super Cup

title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
description: Image source, The Boston Globe/Getty ImagesImage caption, Two girls look through their pinhole boxes during the partial solar eclipse in Boston, USA,
body: Image source, The Boston Globe/Getty ImagesImage caption, Two girls look through their pinhole boxes during the partial solar eclipse in Boston, USA, in 2017ByGeorge SandemanWith most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses. And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead. They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.Here are some viewing methods to try instead.Pinhole projector - card, paper and penThe astronomy group suggests creating a pinhole projector, which can be done by making a hole in a piece of card. You can use the tip of a ballpoint pen to push through the centre of it.Holding the card in one hand and a blank piece of paper in the other, face away from the Sun.Then line the card and paper up so that an image of the Sun becomes visible on the paper.This pinhole projector will show you the shadow being cast on the Sun replicated in miniature.Colander - find one in the kitchenInstead of straining vegetables and pasta, you can use a colander to achieve a similar effect to that of the pinhole projector.Eye specialist David Jones, consultant ophthalmologist at the Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust, says this is his favourite way of witnessing an eclipse."If you hold the colander to the Sun and you look away from the Sun, protecting your eyes, you can make not just one picture of the Sun but a hundred all at once."Demonstrating the technique in a video on social media, he clutches a blank piece of paper behind the colander he is holding up.It creates a kaleidoscope of images showing the Sun and the shadow cast on it during the eclipse.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A colander can be used to view the eclipse Pinhole viewer - cardboard box, foil, paperAn empty cereal box is ideal for making a pinhole viewer. It works similarly to the projector but should provide a clearer image.This is because the cardboard box blocks out the surrounding sunshine and allows in only light from the direction of the eclipse.Cut out a piece of paper that fits the bottom of the box. Open the top of the box and tape the cutout to the bottom. This will be the screen on which you see the eclipse.Close the box and tape it shut. On one half of the top of it, cut out a small square so you can see the paper at the bottom with one eye.On the other half, cut out another small square to match. Cut out a piece of foil that is large enough to cover this square.Tape it down over the square and use a pin or needle to poke a hole in the middle of the foil.Standing with your back to the Sun, use one eye to look through the open square.Once you've lined up the hole in the foil with the Sun, you should see an image of it on the screen at the bottom. This is where you'll see the eclipse too.Can I not use my phone?You might be tempted to video the eclipse using your mobile phone but Nasa advises against this., external"To take images when the Sun is partially eclipsed, you'll need to use a special solar filter to protect your camera, just as you'll need a pair of solar viewing glasses (also called eclipse glasses) to protect your eyes."They also say sensors in your phone could be damaged if pointed directly at the Sun. "This is especially true if you're using any sort of magnifying lens attachment on the phone."When the partial eclipse becomes visible in the UK and mainland Europe on Wednesday, it will be in the evening so it will take place low in the sky.For a better view, the Royal Astronomical Society advises you try standing somewhere more elevated than the area around you "with a clear view of the western horizon".Whatever you do, don't look directly at the Sun.Get in touchAre you planning to watch the Perseid meteor shower peak, and how are you preparing?

schema.headline: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses

title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
description: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquak
body: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake. More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday.  While the official death toll remains at 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing. He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses. Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed. In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort. On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed. Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped.In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed.  The mayor of the municipality, Antonio Cadavid, stated that other children ended up with serious injuries, with a total of 30 children referred to care centres.To combat threats of looting, he has also ordered a curfew, coming into effect at 20:00 local time, and lasting until 06:00 on Wednesday morning. Hours after the earthquake hit Pereira, a resident of the Parque Industrial neighborhood, near the city's airport, told BBC Mundo about the shock being experienced in the area."It's impossible to get around the city center. In Bolívar Square (the city's main square), at least one building collapsed. Furthermore, there are structures where buses and trucks are trapped, and people are afraid those structures will collapse as well," he said."We're all in shock. It was really awful."Jorge Eduardo Rojas, mayor of Manizales, said five people had been killed in the city. Sixty buildings in Manizales had partially or totally collapsed. Cautioning about further aftershocks, Rojas urged the public not to share chain messages or social media posts from unknown sources, as they "may contain false or unverified information... which could cause greater concern and alarm among the public".  On Tuesday, help and support continued to be offered to Colombia from the international community. A statement from a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, stated that he "expresses his solidarity with the people and government of Colombia" and that it working to support the government's response.   Spain's Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, reported that 164 Spaniards were still missing.At the moment, he added, there are no reports of injuries or deaths of its citizens.The Trump administration, which backed President Abelardo de la Espriella in his successful election earlier this year, announced this afternoon a donation of $15.5m (£11.5m) to Colombia.Offers of help have also come from Ecuador, Brazil, El Salvador, and Venezuela.

title: Fan tips: Experts advise how best to use yours during a heatwave
description: No air con? Here's how to get the most out of your electric fan ByEsme Stallardclimate and science reporter and George SandemanStruggling to work and
body: No air con? Here's how to get the most out of your electric fan ByEsme Stallardclimate and science reporter and George SandemanStruggling to work and sleep without air con? Your trusty electric fan could help more than you think - but only if you put it in the right place.During the recent heatwaves, social media was full of advice on how to make your fan work harder - but some of it was conflicting. So, to try to clear up any confusion, we asked experts to separate fact from fiction - from which part of your body to direct your electric fan at, to the best room in the house to put it. Keep windows open or closed? The first thing most people will want to know is if opening a window and using a fan at the same time will cool down their home.It depends, says Becci Taylor, a specialist in building physics at the engineering firm Arup.She says it's best to try to keep the air in your home as cool as possible, so you should keep the windows closed during the daytime, when temperatures outside are likely to be at their highest.She recommends drawing curtains and blinds in rooms facing direct sunlight to stop the air inside heating up. "If the air is cooler than your skin temperature, it's going to cool you down even without sweating," she says.You could place a fan in the coldest room and use that to direct its air towards the rest of your home. Though she advises only doing so if you have a reasonably large or powerful fan.If you have a small fan, then it doesn't particularly matter where in the room you place it on a hot day, says Taylor - provided you keep your windows shut. "You just want it to be near you."At night-time, when the air outside is likely cooler than the air in your home, you should consider opening a window and using a fan to bring in the cooler air.Placing the fan next to the open window and pointing it inwards, towards the rest of the room, can help.But pointing the fan towards the window - to try and blow the hot air in your home outwards, as some social media posts advise - isn't particularly useful as you would not get the cooling benefits of having it pointed towards you.Body or face? Where you should point itPointing the fan directly at your face may be tempting during periods of extreme heat, says Prof Mike Tipton from the University of Portsmouth. But he says that will only give you the perception of "thermal comfort" - in other words you will feel cooler but you're not actually cooling as much as you might think.A specialist in human and applied physiology, he says a fan should be directed more broadly at your body and, crucially, placed far enough away so it "provides air movement over the [whole] body".That air movement improves the effectiveness of your sweating, he says, which is caused by your body naturally trying to cool itself down.Using a fan this way works particularly well if you combine it with other methods of keeping your body temperature down, adds Prof Tipton, such as keeping your hands cool and taking tepid showers.However, if you have young children, you should not point a fan directly at them as it could cause dehydration. Instead, you can use the fan to circulate air around the room.Now for an icy blast Putting a bowl of water or ice in front of a fan will also help, Taylor says. That's because the air movement encourages water in the bowl to evaporate, which takes heat out of the air, making the room a little cooler.You can buy fans that come with a misting device, she adds. Taylor says smaller, handheld versions are most effective indoors.Too much mist increases humidity, which reduces your body's ability to sweat and cool down as there's more moisture in the air. Buying a version that is too large means "you just end up with a very sweaty, damp room", she says."Sweating and misting work in the same way, which is also why it's comfortable and cooler to be near a fountain or open body of water," she says."You can harness that mechanism by putting some liquid in front of the fan, which can evaporate."One important tip is never cover your fan with a wet or frozen towel to try and achieve the same effect, as some social media posts demonstrate, as it can cause electrical safety problems.The 35C debateYour body's temperature is about 37C, while your skin is likely to be about 34C.When the air temperature in your home is less than this a fan is helping you sweat, feel cooler and take away heat from the skin.As the air temperature moves above this, Taylor says a fan can still help to evaporate your sweat - as long as it is not too humid - but it will also bring more heat to your skin.The government advice is not to use a fan once it exceeds 35C inside.Met Office scientists have said there is an increasing likelihood of extreme temperatures in the UK, and that the chance of exceeding 40C is accelerating.Taylor adds: "If people can understand how the physiology of cooling works, then we can start to help them deal with the heat better."Illustrations by Jodi Lai.

schema.headline: Fan tips: Experts advise how best to use yours during a heatwave

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Andy U-turns on early release' and 'Hunt on for eclipse glasses'
description: The Times leads, external on the letter signed by policing leaders to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, to request extra safeguards for the government's pr
body: The Times leads, external on the letter signed by policing leaders to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, to request extra safeguards for the government's prison early release scheme. The paper notes the significance of the letter, which was signed by all 43 chief constables in England and Wales. The Daily Telegraph says, external the letter is "unprecedented", and reveals forces' anger at the possibility that the killers of PC Andrew Harper could walk free under the scheme. The Guardian focuses, external on the warning from the trade union for probation officers, Napo, that the scheme could increase the risk of inmates being released by mistake.The prime minister has said middle class areas will have to "play their part" and take in more migrants, according to the Daily Mail, external. Its report says the announcement came as small-boat arrivals under Andy Burnham hit 3,000 in his first 22 days in power.The i Paper warns, external of rising costs for groceries such as bread, broccoli and steak because of the drought conditions hitting much of England and Wales. It says that puts more pressure on food and drink manufacturers, already facing higher prices as a result of the wars in Ukraine and Iran.A report in the Financial Times, external says car-part makers in China have quietly amassed greater control of Europe's supply chains, leaving the industry wary. According to the paper, Chinese companies have invested in more than 130 European automotive-parts makers since the mid-2000s, in response to growing resistance to its exports.The actress, Lucy Davis' revelation that she has terminal cancer leads the Daily Mirror, external. Its front page features a picture of Davis alongside her co-stars from The Office. The Sun quotes, external her saying she is "at peace" with the diagnosis.Shops across the country have reported selling out of protective eyewear, ahead of tonight's solar eclipse, according to the Metro, external. "The Black Wednesday shopping scramble", reads its headline. The paper says in some cases, people queued for hours to get a pair of glasses and still left empty-handed.

title: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather
description: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 25 June 2026A period of extreme heat across the UK this week has broken records for the hottest day and night temper
body: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 25 June 2026A period of extreme heat across the UK this week has broken records for the hottest day and night temperatures ever recorded in June.It can be hard to sleep during periods of hot weather, but these simple tips could help. 1. Don't let yourself napHot weather can make you feel tired and lethargic during the day. That is because you are using more energy to regulate your internal temperature.But if your sleep is disturbed at night, try to avoid napping during the day. When it is hot, feeling sleepy can be precious - save it for bedtime.2. Keep to your normal routinesHot weather can encourage you to change your habits. Don't. That can disrupt your sleep patterns. Try to keep to your usual bedtime routine, and do the things you normally do before bed.3. Remember the basicsTake steps to make sure your bedroom is as cool as it can be at night.During the day, close the curtains or blinds to keep out the sun. Make sure you shut the windows on the sunny side of your home, to keep out hot air.Open all the windows before you go to bed, to get a through breeze.4. Use thin sheetsReduce your bedding but keep covers handy. Thin cotton sheets will absorb sweat. Wearing loose-fitting clothes made of natural fibres like cotton or linen can keep you cooler than sleeping naked. However hot it is in your bedroom, your body temperature will fall during the night. That is why you sometimes wake up feeling cold even though the temperature is higher than usual. 5. Use a fan and chill your socksUsing even a small fan can be sensible in hot weather, especially when it is humid.It encourages the evaporation of sweat and makes it easier for your body to regulate your internal temperature.If you don't have a fan, try filling a hot water bottle with ice cold liquid instead.Alternatively, cool socks in the fridge and put those on. Cooling your feet lowers the overall temperature of your skin and body.6. Stay hydratedYou should make sure you drink enough water throughout the day but should avoid drinking very large amounts before bed.Image source, Getty ImagesIt's about striking the right balance. You don't want to wake up thirsty - but you don't want to have to take an additional trip to the bathroom in the early hours either.7. But think about what you drinkBe careful about soft drinks. Many contain large amounts of caffeine, which stimulates the central nervous system and makes you feel more awake.Avoid drinking too much alcohol as well. Many people drink more when the weather is hot.Alcohol might help you fall asleep but it also promotes early morning waking and a poorer quality of sleep overall.8. Stay calm - and leave your phone aloneIf you are struggling to sleep, get up and do something calming. Try reading, writing, or even folding your washing.But avoid using your phone. Mindless scrolling might seem appealing, but the blue light from the screen can stimulate your brain and leave you feeling more awake. Return to bed when you feel sleepy.9. Keep to the usual bath and bed times for childrenChildren are often quite robust sleepers - but they can be very sensitive to changes in family "mood" and routine.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lukewarm baths can help before bedtime during hot weatherMake sure usual bedtimes and bath times do not go out of the window just because it is warm.As part of the bedtime routine, the NHS UK website, external recommends lukewarm baths. Make sure they are not too cold, as that will boost your child's circulation which could increase their temperature.A baby cannot let you know if they are too hot or too cold, so it is important to monitor their temperature. They generally sleep best when their bedroom temperature is between 16C and 20C - use a room thermometer to check. 10. Remember that you will be OKMost of us need about seven to eight hours of good-quality sleep each night to function properly.Teenagers, children and babies typically need more sleep because they are still growing.But remember that the majority of people can still function well after a night or two of disturbed sleep.Although you might yawn a little more frequently than usual, you will probably be fine.These tips were based on suggestions by Prof Kevin Morgan, former director of the Clinical Sleep Research Unit at Loughborough University, and Lisa Artis, of the Sleep Council. This article was first published in July 2019.

schema.headline: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather

title: Sun-tanned cauliflowers and knobbly spuds - the heatwave veg that's good to eat
description: Image source, OddboxByAlex DanielBusiness reporterWould you buy a cauliflower that looks like it's been sunburnt or a cucumber that's curled back on i
body: Image source, OddboxByAlex DanielBusiness reporterWould you buy a cauliflower that looks like it's been sunburnt or a cucumber that's curled back on itself?Farmers across the UK are grappling with one of the driest, hottest growing seasons in decades. Repeated heatwaves after a warmer than usual spring have led to predictions of the worst harvest since records began.The heat is not only affecting how much produce is grown, but also how it looks.Retailers usually reject fruit and vegetables that don't meet strict guidelines on size, shape and colour. But with supplies under pressure, many are now expected to loosen those rules rather than risk empty shelves.That means shoppers could start seeing smaller, wonkier or oddly coloured veg on the shelves in the coming weeks - and sellers and growers say it's still good to eat.'Sun-tanned' cauliflowersImage source, OddboxImage caption, This year's extreme heat is turning cauliflower heads yellow rather than whiteCauliflower is one of the most affected vegetables in hot weather because it needs lots of water.Its heads are usually shielded from sunlight by the leaves, but in this year more light is reaching them and turning them yellow.Emilie Vanpoperingh, co-founder of Oddbox, a subscription company that sells surplus produce that supermarkets reject, said it is "purely a cosmetic defect" and the plants taste exactly the same. She said Oddbox acquired 6,000 cauliflower heads last week that were too dark for supermarkets to sell.Growers are reporting that their water reserves are depleted, Vanpoperingh said, which means the cauliflower and broccoli family of brassicas will experience slower growth, leading to shorter supplies.That short supply means retailers may soon start stocking "sun-tanned" cauliflower because "their biggest nightmare is empty shelves", she said. "They want to make sure that they've got availability of produce all the time."Curly cucumbersImage source, Tony Charrin / OddboxImage caption, Extreme heat is also causing cucumbers to curl back in on themselvesGrowers are also reporting cucumbers that are coming out misshapen, with some bending back into a spiral.That is because the plants are grown in greenhouses which overheat in the high outdoor temperatures, causing the plants to become stressed, Vanpoperingh said."Even if they get the irrigation then it's just extreme heat, which means the plant is not able to grow anymore."Holey pak choiImage source, John HarperImage caption, Pests that do well in the heat are eating holes in the leaves of John Harper's pak choiJohn Harper, a farmer in Worcestershire, grows pak choi for Sainsbury's, Aldi and Co-op, and has discarded more produce than usual this year because of tiny holes made by pests.Flea beetles thrive in hot, dry conditions, and farmers are no longer allowed to use as many pesticides as before, meaning net covers are Harper's only defence.Supermarkets' strict cosmetic rules mean "one tiny little hole can render the plant useless", he said, but some have temporarily loosened the rules."We've been working with them through this hot period and in general they sort of get it," he added. Harper said the vast majority of affected pak choi is still edible - even if "it seems to be quite tasty" for the beetles too.Knobbly potatoesImage source, Lucy MunnsImage caption, Hot weather can cause potatoes to grow into several separate sectionsLucy Munns, a potato farmer in Cambridgeshire, said the hot weather will stunt the root vegetable's growth, leading to oddly shaped tubers that supermarkets and chip shops, which she supplies, wouldn't normally buy.When the weather gets cooler after a hot period, instead of the main potato tuber growing "it tends to grow a little knobble on the end"."Trying to find people that will accept potatoes like that is very difficult. So that ultimately means a lot of wastage for us," Munns added. "It's criminal, to be honest, to be chucking that much food away."Those "knobbly and misshapen potatoes" however are absolutely fine to eat, she said."The only difficulty is peeling them, but just cut the knobbly bit off and peel it separately."'A challenging period'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Many supermarkets have started their own 'imperfect veg' lines in recent yearsSupermarkets including Sainsbury's, Tesco, Morrisons and Waitrose already have dedicated lines for wonky vegetables.Calum Kelly, Waitrose's produce technical manager, said in demanding weather conditions "we relax size and shape guidelines for key veg to avoid waste and provide more income to our growers and farmers"."Baking potatoes might be a little smaller than usual this harvest if the drought continues. All these veg still taste great, but like many of us in a heatwave, they might just look a little less than perfect."Not every gap can be filled this way though. Andrew Opie, the director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium, said supermarkets are also importing more food from abroad as UK supplies run short."Retailers face the dilemma of supporting British farmers, but also making sure that we, as customers, have what we expect to buy when we go in the shop," he said."It's going to be a challenging period right through into the autumn. We're hearing potentially it could affect things like cherries as well."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Supermarkets are being forced to import more produce from abroad because of the heatBritish summers are getting hotter and drier as the climate changes and heatwaves like this one are becoming more frequent. That means a season like this one may become less of a one-off, and more of a preview of what British farming has to deal with regularly.Many farmers will either have to accept more waste, invest in better irrigation and water storage systems, or find a way to sell more wonky produce to consumers.Munns, the potato farmer, said more people should try buying imperfect veg if they see it in the supermarket aisle this year.People should "be a bit less picky" about fresh produce, she said. "We've been too spoilt in the UK … In other less fortunate countries we wouldn't have a choice."Get in touchAre you involved in the agriculture industry, or do you have a related story to share?

title: Burnham admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at furth
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support. Burnham told BBC's Wake up to Money he will deliver an "accumulation of smaller things" that "combine to take the pressure down" on household budgets.He spoke of an overhaul of train fares and "more public control" of energy, water and housing but did not give details on how he would bring this about.Burnham has made a number of announcements to help people with the cost of living since taking office, including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to 'subscription traps'.Asked whether the changes he had announced were not significant to people struggling, he said: "I can accept criticism that this isn't enough, because I wouldn't say it's enough."But I take an approach to politics where I do what I can, when I can. Just take that little bit of pressure off and address an issue that you know needs addressing. "It's not the end of the story," he added.The prime minister, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, said he believed "more public control of essential services" such as water, energy and housing, "would mean we could get to a more substantial answer to the cost of living crisis".On water, he said it would not be easy to reverse the privatisation of water companies in England and Wales that took place in the 1980s. "But very much, I'm looking at what can be done. Same with energy."He also said that, following the return of rail operators to public ownership, he wanted to "remodel the rail fares so that we can get more public benefit for people".It comes as the government said on Wednesday that people living within 1,600ft (500m) of new upgraded electricity pylons and substations across Britain will receive a £250 annual discount on their bills for a decade. Burnham told the BBC he has asked Chancellor John Healey to look at what the government can do further on the cost of living in the upcoming Budget, on 28 October, and that Healey has said it will be his "main focus". Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.One major think tank recently warned that he will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet Burnham's pledges on defence and the cost of living.Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people — including income tax, VAT and National Insurance Contributions (NICs) - which Burnham has said he will uphold.He will likely face pressure to address rising costs for businesses, after previous budgets under Rachel Reeves saw employer's national insurance and minimum wages go up.Last month Burnham said pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England would be given a 20% cut to business rates from April, calling it a "first step" to help the industry.He told the BBC he accepted the national insurance hike had added pressure on businesses, and that the government would look at business rates "more broadly".Burnham said: "I would like to bring down the cost of doing businesses. I want to make high streets more vibrant across the country. I know that cannot be done by simply wishing it."But he said he did not want to "at this point, start making commitments"."Those are for the Budget."

schema.headline: Burnham admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support

title: How affordable are Edinburgh's festivals?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByAimee Stanton and Andrew PickenBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoEdinburgh is home to one of the world's biggest cultural eve
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByAimee Stanton and Andrew PickenBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoEdinburgh is home to one of the world's biggest cultural events every summer as it is transformed into a festival city.The Scottish capital hosts the Fringe, the International Festival and the Military Tattoo alongside film, art and book festivals during August.Complaints about soaring prices in the city are nothing new – but recent years have seen increasing concerns about the cost of attending its summer festivals.So how affordable is the city for acts and audiences? BBC Scotland has analysed some of the main costs for festival-goers to see if they really are paying more.Feeling the impact of rising costsImage caption, Kaitlyn Smith says a day out at the festivals has become more expensiveKaitlyn Smith has attended the Fringe every year since moving to Edinburgh from Orkney 10 years ago.She has worked handing out flyers as a way to offset the expense of seeing a range of performances over the course of a day.The 25-year-old said the cost was the "biggest barrier" to local people getting the full festival experience."A full day out at the Fringe, you can spend £100 or £200 in a day," she said."If you are coming on holiday, you know you are coming to the Fringe. You know that you are saving up money to see it, but we're here the whole month and obviously we would like to try and do the Fringe as well."But you are paying £7 or £8 for a pint, £10 or £12 for food - that's one meal. And that's not even starting on your tickets for shows."She added: "I think the shows are worth it, but if you want to see a big volume, you just can't."What makes the city so expensive?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Royal Mile is one of the city's popular destinations during the festivalsDarren Neale, venue director at Greenside Venue in Edinburgh, told BBC Scotland that almost every cost associated with running a Fringe venue had increased significantly over the years.He said utilities, insurance, technical equipment, transport and other operational costs had risen for the venue - but housing had seen the most dramatic change."The cost of staying in Edinburgh during August has risen exponentially over the last decade, creating challenges not only for performers but also for the staff and freelancers who make the festival possible," he said."We have seen our accommodation cost rise on average by 300% in the last decade."He added: "The festival's affordability is one of the reasons it has become the world's largest arts festival, and there is a real balance to be struck between paying people fairly, covering rising costs and keeping live theatre within reach of audiences."How much have accommodation costs increased?The price of finding somewhere to stay during August has long been an issue for the city and its festivals.A slump in Fringe sales in 2022 was blamed on rising accommodation costs but sales recovered in the subsequent years, topping 2.6 million last year.Earlier this year the city lost the TV festival to Manchester, with organisers citing challenges around "accessibility, affordability and sustainability".Figures shared with BBC Scotland from commercial real estate data group Costar suggest average hotel prices have been growing year on year since 2019.The average daily room rate in 2025 was just over £260, an increase of 9% on the previous August and 64% on pre-Covid levels. In comparison, the rate was £110 in Glasgow and £81 in Manchester.Staying in self-catering accommodation is not much cheaper.Figures from Visit Britain suggest renting an entire property in Edinburgh to sleep one or two people cost visitors £204.68 a day in August in 2025. The Glasgow rate was £161.67 and it was £106.92 in Manchester.However, the price for a short-term let can vary dramatically depending on the type – such as a private or shared room within property or booking an entire home - and the number of people.Visitors staying in Edinburgh this year will also have to pay the city's new tourist tax - an additional 5% on top of their original booking cost for the first five nights.Due to a lack of publicly available data, we were unable to analyse festival accommodation costs at university-run establishments.Last year 1.5 million tickets were bought by people with an Edinburgh postcode, up from 1.4 million in 2024.But high housing costs for those living in the city are not restricted to August. Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), external suggests the capital boasts some of the highest average rents in the country.What about the price of tickets?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Gilded Balloon at Teviot is one of the biggest Fringe venuesBut what about the cost of going to shows?We analysed the average price of the cheapest ticket at the six August festivals - nearly 600,000 shows since between 2016 and 2026 - to explore if prices have changed over the last decade.Our analysis found average ticket prices (excluding booking fees) increased in cash terms from £10 to £12.80.When adjusted for inflation, the price of this year's cheapest ticket has actually fallen over the last decade. The figure is £1.37 less than it was 10 years ago, when the average cost was £14.17.Sticking with real terms, average prices of the cheapest ticket were slightly higher before the pandemic but have broadly stayed around £12.75 since 2021 - despite the rising overheads for performers, production companies and venues.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ticket prices make for an interesting picture in EdinburghThe figures also vary by festival.Over the last decade the average lowest ticket price increased in real terms from £19.83 to £20 at Edinburgh International Festival.However, there has been a real term decrease at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, from £14.17 to £12.80.Real term prices have fallen from £17 to £15.50 at the Edinburgh International Book Festival and from £14.17 to £12 at the Edinburgh International Film Festival.Due to the nature of the event, tickets for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo are generally more expensive than other shows.Our analysis found it saw the largest increase, with average lowest ticket prices rising by 36% from £35.41 to £48.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tickets for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo have risen over the last decadeLori Anderson is the director of Festivals Edinburgh, an umbrella organisation for the major city festivals.She said that they are still seen as "incredible value for money" by residents and visitors alike."Costs across Edinburgh in August have risen significantly, particularly accommodation, and our festivals are actively grappling with those issues - albeit with no direct control over them," she explained."What we do control, however, are the events that happen every year."Our festivals work tirelessly to ensure tickets remain affordable for as many people as possible, putting in place ticket offers and concession prices for those who might otherwise feel excluded."Festivals Edinburgh has estimated that the events contribute £852m to Scotland's economy, external every yearAnderson added: "We cannot be complacent - our festivals want to work with partners across the city to ensure that Edinburgh is a city where everyone can afford to live, visit and perform."About the ticket sales dataUsing official listings data from Festivals Edinburgh we analysed the median lowest publicly advertised full price ticket from 2016 to 2026. Prices were adjusted for inflation using Office for National Statistics, external data to allow for comparisons over time. In the absence of ticket sales data, this allowed us to consistently measure like-for-like prices for each event, while reducing the impact of different pricing structures and models across the festivals.The analysis does not account for tickets that may have been sold at a lower price due to promotions, nor concession tickets. Pay-what-you-can, free shows and cancelled events were excluded from the analysis, as were booking fees. The analysis only includes shows that took place in June, July or August.Additional reporting from Isobel Cottam and James Delaney.
